page: UpCloud 80xCPU-512GB is a general-purpose server instance powered by the KVM hypervisor. It features an AMD EPYC 7543 processor with 80 physical cores and 80 vCPUs operating at a base frequency of 2.0 GHz. The CPU architecture is x86_64, utilizing a single thread per core configuration with shared CPU allocation. Memory capacity is 512.0 GB, providing approximately 6.4 GB of RAM per core. Local storage is bundled with a 2048 GB SSD, and the instance includes one complimentary public IPv4 address. No GPU accelerators are present on this server type.

In benchmark evaluations, the server demonstrates top-tier multi-core processing capabilities, placing in the top 10% for multi-core CPU performance under stress-ng, multi-threaded bzip3 decompression, and PassMark CPU encryption and physics tests. Single-core performance is strong, ranking in the top 25% for stress-ng single-core tests and PassMark CPU scores. Memory performance is mixed; while cached small-block read bandwidth and large-block write bandwidth are strong, uncached large-block read bandwidth and overall PassMark memory scores fall into the average tier. Database operations, including Redis SET operations and PassMark database tests, perform strongly, whereas LLM text generation tasks using larger models show performance limitations, with 7B model text generation falling into the bottom 25%.

From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, the 80xCPU-512GB instance offers high resource density, combining substantial compute cores with a large memory footprint and bundled SSD storage. This configuration is highly suitable for multi-threaded workloads that can leverage the high physical core count, such as software compilation, parallel data decompression, and database operations. However, the shared CPU allocation model may introduce performance variability under sustained, non-bursty compute loads. It is best suited for large-scale web serving, database hosting, CI/CD compilation pipelines, and parallel processing tasks, while being less optimal for GPU-dependent workloads or real-time LLM text generation.
